One of my first big forays into tape archiving was back in 2005, when I discovered that atari2600.com had a large collection of Astrocade tapes, including many completely unarchived L&M games.  I bought the ones that we didn't already have on-line, and sent in recordings--all 300 baud--to put on Bally Alley.  This was, of course, before there were any 300 baud processing tools, so these were just raw recordings.  Sometimes what I sent in was exactly what I recorded from the tape.  Other times I fixed loading errors by hand and saved it back out.

One thing I noticed was that, in a few cases where I'd gotten a program that we already had in 2000 baud format, the code was  sometimes significantly different.  So, awhile later, I purchased the remaining tapes there, mostly L&M games that we already had in 2000 baud format.  And after that, 300 baud processing tools became available.  So now, I've went back to the tapes and redone them,  getting everything digitally processed and fixing any errors that could possibly have occurred before.  Mostly, I was able to just run  them through wav2wav, but occasionally I ended up using KCS.  After great frustration, I also managed to type in the 300 baud version of Meteoroid, as detailed previously.  And I went through a small number of recordings from Mike White and Brett Bilbrey to get a couple more programs.

And here are details on some of the games, often taken from my old messages.

Ayatollah Dartboard--We already have this in 2000 baud. The code's a
bit different, but it's pretty much the same.

Claim Jumpers--This is one of Adam's favorite BASIC programs. This has also been converted to cartridge format, and Lance has a 2000 baud tape.  It's just like the pencil and paper game where players take turns drawing lines on a grid and try to complete the most squares. As long as you keep completing squares, you can keep drawing lines.

Color Organ, Light Show Demo--This was designed to work with the L&M
interface. According to the FAQ, "Interface Bally to any stereo amp
with audio power 1 watt on up. TV displays in step with your stereo
music." Does anyone have one of these? Even without it, it still
displays various graphical effects (kind of like a screen saver).  Another program simply labeled "Light Show Demo." is quite similar,  but the menu has a few different effects.

Coyote-Roadrunner Desert Race--I'm not sure this is really working correctly, though it appeared to archive without errors.  It's a two player game, and is supposed to have three screens.  On the first screen, each player can race (extremely slowly) to clear out what look like maybe piles of birdseed.  Pull the trigger and the program will check to see if you've eaten everything, then go off the right side to reach the second screen.  This has cacti instead of birdseed, but pulling the trigger no longer does anything, and I couldn't progress to the third screen even after clearing everything.

Fox And The Hare--It's a two player game in which the hare tries to
hide from the fox. I wish this had come with instructions; as it is
only an examination of the source code revealed how it controlled.
First, choose between 1 and 75 tries. Then, a series of 40 numbers,
randomly chosen from 1 to 60, are displayed. The hare can hide on
either the top or bottom of any of these numbers. Look at the
available hiding places, then hit GO. Press 2 or 3 to choose between
top or bottom, when enter the number to hide in and hit GO. Vertical
blanking is used to hide the number you input. Then the fox chooses
where to look, using controller 1. Hit up or down on the joystick to
look at the top or bottom, then twist the knob and pull the trigger to
select the number to look in. If the fox picks the right hiding
place, it wins. If not, the hare hides again. Either do the same
thing, or hit 0 to stay in the same hiding place. The hare cannot
hide in areas the fox has already looked. Repeat this until either
the fox finds the hare or uses up all of its tries.

Kill The Vulcan--Try to kill the attacking "allien" before you're
"vulcanized." You have artillery on the left of the screen. Adjust
your aim with the knob and pull the trigger to fire. Smaller angles
go further. The enemy tank keeps moving closer, and when it gets
close enough its shots will hit you.

Light Show Program #2--This is another program designed for the L&M
Interface.

Mission Impossible--The ones from atari2600.com and from Mike White are different.  I've labeled the one from Mike White as the alternate version.

Multi. Program Format--Surprisingly, Mike White's master software list
doesn't mention this. It's simply a template for putting a menu into
a BASIC program.

Phantom Star Fighters 2003--We already have this in 2000 baud format,
but it's a fun game. Two players move through a maze trying to shoot
each other, but they're invisible until they fire. If you fire too
many times, you have to pause to reload, making you very vulnerable.

The Black Lagoon--We already have this in 2000 baud format, though
I've confirmed that the code is different. As you move through the
maze, your boat takes on water. When you enter a new area, you can
press the trigger to empty the boat, but be sure to move on before the
patrol boat catches you. If you take on too much water, you sink.
Hint--move diagonally when possible.

The Black Lagoon II--This also isn't on the software list, but was found in with Brett's tape collection.  While the code is different  from the original, it plays extremely similarly.

Rescue Air Drop--Save the troops by dropping supplies onto the
mountaintop. Pay attention to the wind velocity. Unfortunately,
there seems to be no way to dodge the ground forces taking pot shots
at you.

Search And Destroy--Pick numbers to attack so you can randomly destroy
the enemy before it randomly destroys you.

Sink The U-Boat--Very similar to Search And Destroy.

Space Checkers--This is one of my favorite BASIC games. The board is
a grid in which the edges have two types of alien head tokens on them,
and the center and corners have 'N' tokens on them. The first player
places the checker on any of the N spaces, then the players take turns
moving it. You can move the checker to any bordering square
(including diagonally), but once you've moved onto a square, it's
cleared and you can't move there again. Decrease your opponent's
score by clearing the matching alien pieces. At some point, the
checker will be trapped and the game ends, and whoever has the most
alien pieces left wins. (It can be a draw.) There's some serious
strategy to this game, though I recommend playing with a real person
instead of the computer.

Space Quest 2001--We already have this game in 2000 baud format. Turn
the knob to move up and down, and pull the trigger to fire.

Space Sleuth--It's like Clue...in space. And at one point,
it draws a neon green symbol on a bright yellow background, which you're supposed to read by wearing special glasses.

Star Base 2000---Move your ship through the maze to reach the Star
Base. You can cool your engine periodically, but lose points for
doing so. And be sure not to fly into the invisible, completely
undetectable black holes.

Super Sleuth--This is nearly identical to Space Sleuth.

Target (Trio Of Games)--This is a simple but fun game. Score points by firing on blinking boxes, skeet, and a hapless duck. Aim with the knob and fire with the trigger.  You have to hit a very precise area on the target.

I'll e-mail Adam the games--32 programs compressed into just 1MB.

10263:
I got in the mood to knock out some more tape archiving this weekend, and was able to fairly quickly get some Sebree's Computing programs ready.  I had some recordings of these from the Bob Fabris collection as well as Brett Bilbrey's tapes.  Many of these had errors when processing them, though, so it's fortunate that the source code for some of them was available on-line.

First, I archived the programs from their XY Tutorial, which demonstrates how to use the XY command, including achieving some rudimentary perspective:

http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/xy_tutorial.pdf

Demonstration Program #2 on page 5 has a program, and then some additions to the program.  The tape just had the program followed by the additions, but I've archived a version both with and without the extra lines.  The tape didn't include the short program on page 7, but I went ahead and typed it in, calling it Demonstration Program #4.  Finally, there's a cool flight-simulation type program.

Biorhythms & Moon Landing was a joint release by Cursor and Sebree's Computing.  Along with the two programs, it includes a title screen for the tape.  Moon Landing is probably the most sophisticated version of a Lunar Lander-style game I've seen for the system.  After landing, you have to take off and dock with another ship, which is pretty tricky.

Adam had mentioned the wumpus games, of which there are several for the Astrocade.  I've archived Super Wumpus by Sebree's Computing.  I managed to nab the wumpus without falling into a bottomless pit.

Down The Trench portrays an attack on the Death Star.  If there's any strategy to avoiding the enemy lasers, I didn't figure it out.  But I did finally beat it on an easy difficulty.  It's fairly intricate in that it has two stages to the game, plus an ending animation.

Star Fire is a cockpit-perspective space shooting game.  I found it difficult to locate the enemy ships, however. You only need to specify the number of bytes when you :PRINT. When you :INPUT it
will input until it sees the the EOF marker put on the tape.
So, your save should be...
:PRINT ;:PRINT @(x), n     or :PRINT ;:PRINT %(aaaaa),n    where the x is the
starting array number, n is the number of WORDS to be saved, and aaaaa is the
address to start at. each @(x) uses one WORD.
To input the info use .....
:INPUT ;:INPUT @(x);RUN    or    :INPUT ;:INPUT %(aaaaa);RUN
It would then load the bodt of the program and either the @(x) string,  or the
addresses until done, and then start the program.
Any questions?
Ken

Ken Lill wrote:

Now that I have moved to Blue Ash, Ohio, It is not easy to ask Mike any more. His work/sleep hours are usually crazy. But I'll try to email him.
>>

I managed to contact Mike White, and he put me onto the information that allowed me to solve the saving/loading problem with "Maze Avenger."  It really helps that I just recently learned how to make an autorun AstroBASIC program, as the technique to do both is nearly identical.  Not everyone here will care for the following full explanation, but I'm writing it to the group in case it is of some use in the future.  Now it will be in the archives and a search will being up the fix if anyone is looking for it (or I forget how it's done).

First off, Mike gave me a solution that was right except for the syntax.  For the correct syntax, I had to use his BASIC Tutorial, "Tricks of the Trade #3," available here,

http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/tutorials/tricks_of_the_trade_03.pdf

This gives an explanation of AutoRun and why it works.  This same EXACT technique is used to eliminate the "WHAT?" loading error.

First, here is how to solve the trouble that will work with just about any program (perhaps all program), as it saves all of RAM:

PRINT ";STOP";:PRINT %(16384),2000

That's it.  Now the program loads and doesn't give the error message.  If you recall, in order to have an AutoRun program, you type this command:

PRINT ";RUN";:PRINT %(16384),2000

Very similar!

However, we're being very heavy handed with this solution.  It works, but we don't really HAVE to save everything.  We just want to save the BASIC program and the machine language routine.  "Maze Avenger's" ML Routine begins at:

20237 = $4F0D

The ML routine is stored through:

20278 = $4F36

We really only need to save from $4000-$4F36 (+1 Word, for the End of File Marker).  We can figure out EXACTLY what needs to be saved with a few simple calculations:

1) Calculate the number of bytes required: $4F36 - $4000 = $0F36 = 3894 bytes

2) Figure out how many words are needed by dividing the number of bytes by two: 3894 / 2 = 1947

3) Account for the End of File Marker: 1947 + 1 = 1948

If you don't account for the EOF Marker, then you're going to clobber the last word of your ML routine.

The following command will save EXACTLY what is needed:

PRINT ";STOP";:PRINT %(16384),1948

I can't think of any reason why saving all of RAM (2000 words) wouldn't work all of the time.  Yet, it IS nice to know a little bit about what is going on and how to save EXACTLY what you want saved.

Thanks to everyone that chipped in to help solve this problem.

Side 1 starts with Graphic Character Maker as described.  The handwritten note is indeed hard to read, but gives some directions.  Directions are typed out in the newsletter (Arcadian volume 3, issue 12, page 128), so check these if you're interested.

Graphic Character Maker appears to have been recorded over (Mortgage) Amortization, leaving only the end of the program.  While this has been archived, the code on the tape is different.  Since only the end is left, I won't try to turn this into a working program, but here is the remaining code:

Side 2 starts out with Sampler #3.  This is actually a somewhat important find, because the only recording I had of it (from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection) had some loading errors I had to fix by hand.  Line 2000 sets a variable C to serve as a counter for the number of cycles, but I was unable to tell what it was initialized to.  I initialized it to 0, but it turns out it should actually be set to 1.  This won't have a dramatic effect on the program operation, but it will change it, so I'll redo this program.

Next is Clock, which is identical to the archived version.  Next is Code Breaker, but this is actually an alternate version.  Finally, TV Ghost is identical to the archived version.

These recordings processed easily, but for future reference, I recommend avoiding clipping.  You can't make use of the high pass filter if the peaks are clipped.

Hopefully I'll run across some more W&W programs in my own collection, since there are still a couple missing.

10311:
I added Richard Degler's updated source code of the "300 To 2000 BAUD LOADER PROGRAM."  The version jumped from 1.0 to version 1.2.  The changes and additional comments are:
     
- Sorted the EQUates and added note to "Bit Banger Goodies".

- Used only $xx for code instead of mix of 0xxH and decimal.

- Wow, Adam - you translated this from TDL's 8080 mnemomics!

- Assembler's "non-standard syntax" warning was for "ADD  E" on old line 248 (not sure why the previous line was flagged)

- Corrected two very mino[r] typos in transcribed comments.

- Actually assembled this and compared it to earlier versions.

More note: This program uses the entire screen (past its area) as a huge Tape Buffer (instead of having a small Ring Buffer), only saving lines that are numbered.  Since 300-baud's direct commands (NLN) and .REMarks might have a few numbers in them, these should be edited from the recording if at all possible.

The program source code can be downloaded directly, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/300BLOAD.asm

This program, and how to use it are in the Astro BASIC Manual on Page 104.  You can download the program, in a ready to run 2000-Baud AstroBASIC version, here:

http://tinyurl.com/4q5hs9j

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/basic_manuals/programs_a-m/array_builder_%5Bbasic_manual%5D.zip

You may notice that the program is called "Array."  That's because that is the name that Mike White used when he archived the program (if you read the AstroBASIC manual, then this makes sense).  I need to change this name so that it makes sense to most people, especially since lately I've discovered that this is one of the most useful programs written for AstroBASIC.  So changing the name of the program has been added to my to-do list for BallyAlley.com

Thanks, Richard, for investigating into the machine language world of the Bally/Astrocade.

Enjoy!

Adam
10312:
I have added an archived version of the "Bally BASIC Sampler" tape.  This tape is a true piece of history.  As Dick Ainsworth said right here on this discussion group back in 2002:



"I think that the tape cassette that I wrote for the Bally BASIC
cartridge was the first -- or certainly one of the first -- examples of
personal computer software for the mass market. The cassette with Bill's
 Microsoft BASIC was released at the same time. In fact, I first met
Bill at the GRT recording studio where we were recording masters for the
 Bally BASIC cassette and Microsoft BASIC cassette, so the release dates
 would be nearly identical. I don't know of anyone who had sold personal
 software to a mass market before this. If you have other examples,
please let me know."


Here is what is included:

Side 1:
1. Electric Doily (Graphics)
2. Line Graph
3. Monthly Records
4. Electronic Music
5. Number Match (Guessing Game)

Side 2:
1. Lunar Lander
2. Gravity Game
3. Newtonia '500'

Originally there was a message with the original non-digital archive that said, "NOTE: The original tape has markers for 'Monthly Records' to save its records at/into.  As this is useless when piping tape audio from the computer, they were removed from the recordings to reduce size. This makes 'Monthly Recordings' potentially unusable even if restored to a cassette tape."  Paul: is this still true, or does the digital archive have these markers back in place?

The tape can be downloaded here:

http://tinyurl.com/4au7sja

(or use the full URL:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/misc/Bally%20BASIC%20Program%20Sampler%20(1978)(Bally%20Manufacturing%20Corp)(300%20baud).zip

The original program's non-digital archived size was 5.97 MB.  Digital archiving has reduced this to 124K.  Thanks for archiving this, Paul.

Enjoy!

I also OCR'd the instructions for "Graphic Character Utility."  For a program published in the Arcadian, these instructions are quite lengthy.  It wasn't unusual at all to have a program with a one sentence description of the game-- and this often didn't include how to play!  These instructions are included with the download, but I thought that including them here would be a good idea too.


Graphic Character Utility
By Bob Weber
1981
Source: Arcadian, vol. 3, no. 12 (October 1981), pg. 128.

Instructions
------------

Load the program and RUN it.  The program will draw a 9 x 16 grid on the screen, and there will be a flashing cursor in the bottom left hand corner.  Move the cursor with the joystick, and when you have it located, turn the knob to the right and press the trigger.  This will blacken in a square.  If you want to 'erase,' turn the knob to the left and press the trigger.  When you are satisfied with the character, move the cursor to the right side of the screen and press the trigger.  The machine will now compute the values and load them into a string.  When it is finished, it will display the character in actual size on the screen and ask 'OK?'.  If everything is the way you want it, prepare the tape you are going to use, and press GO.  If it is not the way you want it, press any key other than GO, and you will be back in the character construction mode.

If the computer says 'DOES NOT COMPUTE', it means you have a single pixel placed in the left hand corner of either the left or right half of the drawing. When you do this you cannot load the values onto tape, because the poked value for one pixel at those locations is 32768, too big for the computer.


I wonder how useful "Graphic Character Utility" became to Bally BASIC programmers?  It's better than pencil and paper, that's for certain!

Thanks for archiving this Bob Weber tape, Paul.

I combined Jay Fenton's "Array Builder" and "Array" into one archive with the MUCH more helpful name of "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program."  This program was designed to load 300-Baud Bally BASIC tape recordings into AstroBASIC using AstroBASIC's built-in tape interface.  This allowed using older 300-baud tapes with the new AstroBASIC cartridge without the need to retype the program.  Lately, I have found a better use for it.

I have used the "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program" lately for archiving purposes with fantastic results.  Probably the best use I've found for this program is for typing in AstroBASIC programs into Notepad.  After the AstroBASIC program has been typed into Notepad, I then use "txt2prg" to convert the text file into a file for use with "KCS," a program that converts the file to 300-Baud format, normally for use with the 300-Baud Interface.  However, using "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program," I can instead load the AstroBASIC program directly into AstroBASIC.  I love it.  No need to type on the Astrocade's 24-key keypad anymore.

This archive includes:

1) Full documentation from the AstroBASIC Manual

2) "Array Builder" - Used to input and then save the "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program" to tape.

3) "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program"

To use the conversion program, it is not necessary to use the "Array Builder" at all.  "Array Builder" is included for archive purposes only.

The "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program" can be downloaded from the AstroBASIC Manual Program A-M Program Download Area, here:

http://tinyurl.com/495odab

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/basic_manuals/programs_a-m/programs_a-m.html

Here are the full operating instructions to use the "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program," directly from the AstroBASIC manual:


OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS

     Bally BASIC has a special command for loading machine language programs directly into screen memory, bypassing the BASIC language format entirely.  It is called "COLON-RUN," and is typed in similar to the familiar :INPUT command.  RESET your computer and type:

     :RUN

Load the TAPE CONVERTER PROGRAM you just built, using the :RUN command.  When loaded, the screen background brightness will change continuously.  Cue up the 300 baud tape, press GO, and load the 300 baud program into the computer.  Observe the program statements accumulating in the buffer just below the program zone.  The screen will reveal the scratchpad during this phase.

     Program loading will stop on any of the following conditions:
        (a) :RETURN is found in an unnumbered line.
        (b) RUN is found in an unnumbered line.
        (c) Any other key in the column beneath HALT is pressed.

Cases (a) and (c) will cause the program to go back to the flashing grey scale mode.  Case (b) will cause the program to proceed to final loading.  If you wind up in the grey scale mode and have no more segments to load, press HALT to get to the final loading.  After HALT is pressed, or RUN is found, the program will convert the statements in the buffer into the representation used within your Bally BASIC.  This is done by moving the buffer to the highest possible address and using special I/O routines which feed characters from this buffer to the Bally BASIC Input routines.  This will be seen on the screen as a race between the input buffer and the program storage area.  The CONVERTER PROGRAM will then exit to Bally BASIC.  The variables A to Z will be zeroed out, and the screen will be cleared.  The program may now be executed or written out at 2000 baud.

     NOTE: During the read-in phase, lines without line numbers, rubout characters, and spaces appearing before and immediately after line numbers are filtered out.  It is permissible to load tapes which contain line numbers out of sequence or which delete previous lines.


I've heard many people over the years say that they'd type in a program for AstroBASIC if they could type it on a regular keyboard.  Hopefully some of those people will take advantage of the power of the utilities that have been accumulating over the years for the Bally Astrocade.

Enjoy!

Here are the full operating instructions to use the "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program," directly from the AstroBASIC manual:



OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS



     Bally BASIC has a special command for loading machine language programs directly into screen memory, bypassing the BASIC language format entirely.  It is called "COLON-RUN," and is typed in similar to the familiar :INPUT command.  RESET your computer and type:



     :RUN



Load the TAPE CONVERTER PROGRAM you just built, using the :RUN command.  When loaded, the screen background brightness will change continuously.  Cue up the 300 baud tape, press GO, and load the 300 baud program into the computer.  Observe the program statements accumulating in the buffer just below the program zone.  The screen will reveal the scratchpad during this phase.



     Program loading will stop on any of the following conditions:

        (a) :RETURN is found in an unnumbered line.

        (b) RUN is found in an unnumbered line.

        (c) Any other key in the column beneath HALT is pressed.



Cases (a) and (c) will cause the program to go back to the flashing grey scale mode.  Case (b) will cause the program to proceed to final loading.  If you wind up in the grey scale mode and have no more segments to load, press HALT to get to the final loading.  After HALT is pressed, or RUN is found, the program will convert the statements in the buffer into the representation used within your Bally BASIC.  This is done by moving the buffer to the highest possible address and using special I/O routines which feed characters from this buffer to the Bally BASIC Input routines.  This will be seen on the screen as a race between the input buffer and the program storage area.  The CONVERTER PROGRAM will then exit to Bally BASIC.  The variables A to Z will be zeroed out, and the screen will be cleared.  The program may now be executed or written out at 2000 baud.



     NOTE: During the read-in phase, lines without line numbers, rubout characters, and spaces appearing before and immediately after line numbers are filtered out.  It is permissible to load tapes which contain line numbers out of sequence or which delete previous lines.



I've heard many people over the years say that they'd type in a program for AstroBASIC if they could type it on a regular keyboard.  Hopefully some of those people will take advantage of the power of the utilities that have been accumulating over the years for the Bally Astrocade.



Enjoy!

I was recently sent links to the source code for "Tiny BASIC" for various operating systems and CPUs.  Since "Bally BASIC" and "AstroBASIC" are offshoots of "Tiny BASIC," I thought that they might belong on Ballyalley.com.  However, I'm not sure if this is appropriate or not.  I don't want to get too far away from the Bally Arcade/Astrocade (see last paragraph of this posting for more details about this).

The source code here is for four different CPUs.  The common CPUs that I would expect to see are here: Zilog Z-80, Intel 8080 and
Motorola 6800. There is one true oddball in the bunch though: the National
Semiconductor SC/MP microprocessor.  I'm not even aware of any
microcomputer that ever used this CPU that was released in 1974 (Bill, can you set me straight on this?).  I do
have a book on how to build a computer from component parts using this the SC/MP
CPU-- so SOME people were at least using this CPU... even if on the VERY fringe.

Here's is the various source code available:


1) Lawrence Livermore BASIC and Disk Tiny BASIC [For Z-80, and CP/M in particular].  This collection is from a CP/M disk collection (CPMUG002 - Volume 2).  The description even says that later disks have a newer version of this BASIC.  I, however, don't have those disks.  If someone is interested in the later version, then they will have to find it themselves.

CPMUG002 - Volume 2

Lawrence Livermore BASIC and Disk Tiny BASIC

Note that improved implementations of LLLBASIC and disk Tiny BASIC now are present on volumes 10 and 11 respectively.

NUMBER    SIZE    NAME        COMMENTS

CATALOG.2    CONTENTS OF CP/M VOLUME 2

2.1    84K   LLLBASIC.ASM     LLBASIC INTERPRETER SOURCE
2.2    38K   LLLBASIC.COM     IMPLE PATCHED COM FOR CP/M
                              (NOT ECONOMICAL, BUT INSTRUCTIVE)
2.3    2K    LLLBASIC.DOC     NOTES ON LLLBASIC
2.4    61K   LLLFP.ASM        FLOATING-POINT PACKAGE FOR LLLBASIC
2.5    2K    LLLMON.ASM       KLUGE MONITOR TO TEST LLL IN
             LLLBASIC.COM
2.6    2K    STARTREK.DOC     COMMENTS ON STARTREK.TBI
2.7    6K    STARTREK.TBI     TINY BASIC LOADABLE STARTREK
2.8    3K    TINYBAS.COM      SHERRY VERSION OF WANG PALO ALTO
                              TINY BASIC, WITH DISK SAVE AND
                              LOAD OF PROGRAMS FOR CP/M
2.9    13K    TINYBAS.DOC     FULL INSTRUCTIONS FOR TINYBAS


2)  Robert Uiterwyk's Micro Basic [for 6800 CPU] - I have this in source form.  Also, a man in Germany scanned in the article from "The Best of Interface Age, Vol. I" for me very recently.  So that version is available too.  The scan is OKAY, and readable, but I went ahead and requested this book via Interlibrary loan for two reasons: to rescan the article and source, and because the book itself looks very interesting to me.  Even if no one here is interested in this code, then it will be going on the APF M1000 Programming website that I also have.  Interestingly, this was distributed with the original "Interface Age" magazine as a "Floppy ROM," that is on a record!

Here is some additional information about the exact version that I have.

In June of 1976 the Southwest Technical Products Corp. newsletter contained the source code for several programs. Two were by Robert Uiterwyk, a text editor and a 4k BASIC Interpreter (Bill Turner wrote the manual for BASIC). At the time MITS was going to sell BASIC (by Micro Soft) for $200. SWTPC was going to try to give away its software.

Many people were writing "Tiny BASIC" programs in 1976 and 1977. This program started as one but later grew into a full 8K version and a disk version. SWTPC (Dec 76 BYTE) sold the 4K version for $4.95 and the 8K version for $9.95.

I downloaded this from:
http://www.swtpc.com/mholley/NewsLetter1/

More information is available here:

http://www.swtpc.com/mholley/NewsLetter1/Issue1_Index.htm
http://www.swtpc.com/mholley/NewsLetter1/MicroBasic.htm
http://www.swtpc.com/mholley/BYTE/Dec1976/Dec_1976_BYTE.htm


3) Sherry Brothers Tiny BASIC [For Intel 8080]

This is a copy of Lichen Wang's 'Palo Alto Tiny BASIC' which has been modified to incluude more functions, and disk save and load.  It sets it's size to whatever size your system is, so it does not need to be reassembled for different system sizes.


4) NIBL.ASM - Tiny BASIC for the National Semiconductor SC/MP microprocessor, (NIBL-P, release date 12/17/76)

This file has been prepared via OCR and text editor from the original assembly listing; then re-assembled and rigorously checked for errors.

The following differences exist from the original listing:

- Many original local labels (mostly for short jumps) have been given  new names to insure global uniqueness.

- Macros have been modified (or created) to allow compatibility with a modern, generic, macro-assembler.

- After being passed through the OCR process, neatness of the original text has suffered some cosmetic inconsistency.

Of further note:

- The macro-assembler used here is a free tool, "AS", by Alfred Arnold:
     http://john.ccac.rwth-aachen.de:8000/as/

- The cryptic syntax "./256" used as the operand of the instruction at address 0087 suggests that there may have been "hooks" incorporated for relocation of the NIBL interpreter code. An assembled operand value of zero has been retained as in the original.

- On my original hardcopy listing, hand written notations indicate that the "OR HI(P2)" instructions at addresses 05D3 and 0936 were later changed to "ANI 01". As I recall, this was a minor bug fix that may have been published in a National Semiconductor newsletter or in an issue of Dr. Dobb's Journal.


I understand that this only relates to the Astrocade in the most primitive of ways.  I thought that some techies might be interested in this code (Richard, in particular and perhaps Lance too), but I could be wrong.  This will stay OFF of BallyAlley.com unless a couple of people request it to be added.  In that case... I'm not even sure where I'll put it, but I'll figure SOMETHING out.

10370:
I mentioned in a posting a short while ago that I have a book on how to create a computer from component parts using the National Semiconductor SC-MP Microprocessor.  Perhaps some Astrocade techies might have an interest in how to build a computer from the same CPU used in the Astrocade's: the Zilog CPU.  I understand that BUILDING the computer is probably not on anyone's to-do list, but just glancing through a book like this is pretty neat.

The most recent how-to book on this subject that I have is from 1981.  It is by Steve Garcia (of Byte fame).  The book is
 called "Build Your Own Z80 Computer: Design Guidelines and Application
Notes."  This is the only book that I that own that I've also seen available online.  It's not a pdf though, it's a series of images.  You can read it, or glance it over, here:





http://www.scribd.com/doc/13388965/Build-Your-Own-Z80-Computer




I have several books on building computers from
component parts.  If you type "Build computer from component parts" into
 Google right now then you will find plenty of topics on the subject, but they
 are really all false hits.  Those hits are for how to ASSEMBLE a
computer from parts that you can buy at any computer store.  I'm referring to
 building a computer from transistors, microchips and other electronic components on a board of your
own making.

I suppose that I have about five or six of these books and they all use various CPUs. 
"One of these days" I plan to scan them in and put them on a TINY website
called something like "How to REALLY Build a Computer from Component
Parts."  I would never attempt to build one of these computers, but for
historical interest, these books are rather priceless.  There is just tons of information in these that you won't find anyplace else.

I have one book in particular that has some way-off-the-beaten-path information.  The 544-page book, published in 1978, is called "How to Design & Build Your Own Custom TV Games" by David L. Heiserman.  What makes this book the most unusual out of the whole bunch is that the "TV Games" don't use CPUs at all, nor do they use the Pong-on-a-chip chips that were created and used in most of the "Pong" knockoffs.  The games in this book are completely built from component parts, and they aren't all "simple" games like "Pong" either.  Some games are rather complicated, like "Tank" games, "Golf" and games with animated figures.  There are no screenshots included in the book, which is a bit disappointing.  However, there are TONS of schematics and explanation.  In the end, if you build this, then you would end up with a videogame that I imagine would be similar to how ALL the videogames in the arcade were made before 1975.  I've never seen information like this on the Internet anywhere else before.  I've seen overviews of how to build a videogame, but NEVER without a CPU.


I'm not sure if "one of these days" will ever come for a "Build a Computer from Components" site, but I do think that this is all pretty neat stuff.  I don't understand it, really (it's SO far past my skill level), but I bought these books not to build the games or computers, but to see just where the writers were coming from and how they approached the subject.  That I DO understand.

I just picked up "Best of Interface Age, Volume 1: Software in BASIC" via InterLibrary Loan.  This book was published in 1979.  There is a VERY nice "General Software Index," compiled by Jim Schreier, that covers software published from December 1976 through December 1978.  There are eight programs that are Z80 related.  I've included the introduction to the Index, followed by the Z80-related items and also the 8080-related items:

"Interface Age"
General Software Index

Compiled by Jim Schreier

     The software published in Interface Age between December 1976 and December 1978 is rich and varied.  Historically, this time period marked the apex of "hobbyist" software and the dawning of "business" programs.  Generally, the 1977 pages of Interface Age contained assembled programs for the SC/MP, 6800 and 8080.  The 1978 edition published software for a wider variety of chips plus BASIC, FORTRAN and PILOT programs.  This variety of subject matter will interest most microcomputer users as well as provide a permanent record of excellent software.

     This compilation is divided into two sequential sections: Software by High Level Language and Software by CPU chips.

     The High Level Languages are in alphabetical order by the name of the BASIC.  Most users will want to see what programs were published for their specific microcomputer.  The term "GENERAL BASIC" means the documentation failed to identify a specific BASIC dialect.  Of course, there is no such thing as a "General BASIC," yet.  It is possible to translate one BASIC to another given enough time.

     Likewise, the assembled software is arranged by CPU chips in numeric order.  Some of the most important published software programs appear in this section.  Foremost is the publication in four parts of the Livermore BASIC Interpreter.

I have added "Best of Interface Age: Volume I, Software in BASIC," edited by Carl. D. Warren (copyright 1979) to my APF MP1000 and Imagination machine website.  This is because I first became interested in this book because of Chapter 4, which includes a 6800 4K BASIC.

Anyone in the Astrocade world that is interested in Tiny BASIC will be interested in this book too.  Chapter 2 features Dr. Wangs Palo Alto Tiny BASIC written for the 8080.  Chapter 3 also features a Tiny BASIC with extensions for the National Semiconductor's SC/MP called NIBL.  Unlike Tiny BASIC, which (according to the book) was developed primarily as a games language, NIBL has I/O features and other abilities lacking from typical Tiny BASIC extensions.

You can download the book here:

The scan is a high-quality, 300dpi, B&W, 9MB pdf. I took special care to give this pdf excellent bookmarks for ease of use. The Preface of Volume 1 (see below) references the "Best of" series as having five volumes. Yesterday I requested the second book in the series via InterLibrary Loan: "Best of Interface Age: Volume 2, General Purpose Software."  This book should arrive in a few weeks.  As for the other three books I can not find ANY mention of them ANYWHERE online. I suspect that they may never have been released.  If you know otherwise, then please post about it.

I have included an overview of the book (which I wrote, since one wasn't available), included the preface and a the table of contents:


Overview

What an unusually named book.  With the subtitle "Software in BASIC," the reader would expect to find software written in the BASIC language.  That ISN'T what is included at all.  Instead, this 314 page book includes four BASIC interpreters.  Each program is QUITE lengthy and is written in assembly language for three different 8-bit CPUs that were popular in the mid-to-late 1970's: Intel's 8080, Motorola's 6800, and National Semiconductor's SC/MP.

If you're looking for another book full of BASIC software, then look elsewhere.  If you're interested in early 8-bit CPUs and would like to see how some of the computer pioneers used their often "assembly required" computers then this book is for you.

I've included the preface and the table of contents from the book:


Preface

     Several months ago, it became apparent that we should give serious thought to creating a "best of" series from the pages of Inter-face Age.  The idea seemed like it would not present a major problem at first, until we looked at the mountain of material we had available.  The quantity wasn't the only problem.  The decision had to be made on what was best, so it could be included in the reprint series.
     After careful consideration, with close attention being paid to readers' letters, the decision was made to create a "best of" series of "Interface Age" Classics.  What this meant was that rather than to create a huge, difficult to use book of just about everything, we are printing the classic software pieces and the ones that many readers said they would like to see.
     The four reprinted articles that you find in this volume are those classics.  Furthermore, they represent several different programming techniques.  At the same time, they provide the reader with some of the most useful software ever created.
     Chapter four, "The Great Experiment," offers the one piece of software that has been requested more than any other: the complete source listing of Uiterwyk's 4K BASIC.  It is an absolute classic.  The source code was released into the public domain by Mr. Uiterwyk for this software volume, so students of software could achieve maximum benefit from its use.  For this, we at "Interface Age" are extremely grateful.
     My staff and I are quite convinced that everyone who makes use of this first volume will find it invaluable in making better use of their systems.
     Volume 2 of this series is made up of additional general purpose software from some of the "Interface Age" authors you have enjoyed over the past few years.  Volumes 3 and 4 are dedicated specifically toward the small businessman.  These two volumes contain more business software than any book currently available today.
     To round out this current "best of" series, Volume 5, "Best of Interface Age- Things to Think About," contains those articles for the futuristic thinker and gadgeteer.  This volume contains reprints from Roger Garret's famous "Inventor's Sketchpad." Also included are short and useful software tips, along with some handy hardware articles.
     Interface Age has always been known as the leader in the publication of important and useful software and ideas.  We feel that the publication of this "best of" series will further enhance our leadership and provide you with hundreds of hours of enjoyment.

Carl Warren
Editor-In-Chief


Table of Contents

Chapter 1 - Lawrence Livermore 8080 BASIC
   By Jerry Barber, Royce Eckard, John Dickenson, David Mead,
     and E. R. Fisher
   Original publication date: December 1976, January, February,
     and March 1977

Chapter 2 - Dr. Wang's Palo Alto TINY BASIC
   By Roger Rauskolb
   Original publication date: December 1976

Chapter 3 - National's TINY BASIC-- NIBL
   By Phil Roybal and Mark Alexander
   Original publication date: December 1976, January 1977

Chapter 4 - The Great Experiment-- Floppy ROM # 1
            Robert Uiterwyk's 6800 4K BASIC
   By Bill Turner and William Blomgren
   Original publication date: May, July 1977

Appendix A - General Software Index
   A comprehensive index of general purpose software printed
   in "Interface Age" since January, 1977

Appendix B - Available Back Issues
   A list of all the back issues that are still available, and
   how to obtain them.

Index


Enjoy the book!

Ken Lill pointed out a 9V power supply that would have worked, but since I was going to spend the money anyway, I figured that I would get something a little better.  I wanted a multi-voltagge power supply.  I want to thank Ken for pointing out that the power supply doesn't HAVE to be 6 volts; that a 9-volt adapter will work fine (as long as it supplies at least 500mA).

I initially visited Radio Shack and they no longer carry variable voltage power supplies.  Now they only sell power supplies with ONE voltage AND you have to buy the tip separately for Six dollars (!) each for a total cost of about fifteen dollars.  That is outrageous, especially since those power supplies at Radio Shack are only 500mA and not switching power supplies (just plain old, everyday, run of the mill, wall warts).

I finally decided on a Velleman Compact Universal AC Adapter Power Supply available from Amazon.com.  This supplies 1.5A-- which is really great.  Here are the complete specs:

This regulated power supply from Velleman is versatile enough to handle most any application.
Six selectable voltages allow for use with most hand held or office electronics. Eight tips are included and cover virtually any size jack or plug on the market. Polarity change is accomplished through alternate tip installation. A high current design will supply up to 1.5A and 10 watts max. Features and Specifications: *Regulated DC power output: 3V, 4.5V 6V, 7.5V, 9V, and 12V *Current output: 1.5A max *Supplied tip sizes: 2.5 mm male, 3.5 mm male, 1.35 mm x 3 mm, 1.5 mm x 3.5 mm, 1.7 mm x 4 mm, 2.1 mm x 5 mm, 1.5 mm x 5 mm, 2.5 mm x 5.5 mm.

I purchased the power supply for $19.79 ($24.91 after shipping).  If you're interested, you can purchase it here:

http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00068U44I

I received the power supply a few days ago and I finally got to test it today.  I tested the various voltages with my multimeter and they are RIGHT ON the money.  There didn't need to be a load for the voltage to read "correctly."  I used the new power supply with my Blue Ram and it works perfectly.  I am able to load and save using the 6-Volt setting.  That is, everything is working just as it should.

Now that I have a good power supply I was able to figure-out a problem that I would sometimes have when loading or saving with the Blue Ram.  The trouble turned out to be the dual audio cable that I was using (the original one that came with the Blue Ram).  I couldn't use it reliably even to load AstroBASIC programs.  So, I tossed it.  Problem solved!

Now that I'm I'm back in business does anyone want to write a new game cartridge?!?  I can test it out for ya!

Russ Perry Jr. wrote:

Hey, thanks for the link.  That's actually pretty nice.  I have these dream that someday Google will finally be able to work something out with publishers and ALL back issues of books and magazines will be available.  I'd pay HUNDREDS of dollars a year for a subscription service to something like that.  It would be worth it!

I know that many people don't want to scan their magazines because in order to get a good scan, you usually have to take the magazine apart.  Some magazines, I THINK "Video Games" is one of them, actually are bound with staples rather than glue.  This means that you can scan them and then put them back together.  I really don't blame people AT ALL for not wanting to mess up their magazines.  That's the way that I used to be with my Amiga and Commodore magazines.  Then, one day, I just gave them all away because I had a lack of space.  Those magazines are in good hands, but when I think about it, what difference would it make NOW if I had taken the magazines apart back THAN?  Still, even if no damage WHATSOEVER happened to a magazine, it takes a long time to scan in color.  Black and white books don't don't too long, but to get quality color scans sometimes people's scanners move at a snail's pace.

>>
I was trying to find the copyright holder [...] in hopes of putting together a legal compilation of scans [...]. Perhaps others have thought the same thing, and that's kept free ones out of the public eye.
>>

It's possible.  It's probably even probable.  For instance, after I scanned in the Arcadian newsletters volume 1-6  Bob Fabris sent me all of the issues in pdf format.  Someone had already scanned all the issues for him using a sheet scanner.  This was great because he sent me volume 7, which at the time I didn't know even existed (the last issue of volume 6 says that it's the LAST issue ever... but it wasn't because a new editor took over for a very brief time).  The scans of volume 7 are actually THOSE scans sent to me by Bob.

Now that I have the original documents for Arcadian volume 7, "one of these days" I want to rescan the last volume, as those scans are quite light in certain areas and sometimes the pages are rather crooked.  But, really, what does it matter?  They are good enough for most people-- in fact I've never got one complaint about them.  The scans are certainly good enough for reading.  It isn't like most folks are trying to type-in the programs from those issues.  If anyone ever DOES have trouble with volume 7, then please let me know and I'll rescan certain requested pages.

10425:
Bill Loguidice wrote:
>>
I know many computers from the 70's suffered key bounce (single hits registering as multiple hits)
>>

All keyboards and switches have bounce... it's just a natural phenomenon that CAN'T be avoided.  Their are VERY simple electronics circuits that take care of this.  It can also be taken care of with software.  Recently I noticed that when I press keys in "Color BASIC" they would repeat.  Richard Degler tracked this down to the debounce routine in "Color BASIC" being different from Bally BASIC.  In another example, APF BASIC has a location in memory that can be POKEd to change the debounce time.

>>
I think it would more likely be a degradation of the contacts under the pad, no?
>>

This is true.  Of the several Astrocade units that I've had over the years, many of the keypads have acted slightly differently.  Also, Atari and Commodore keyboards would do the same thing.  As Bill said, you can often "exercise" them and they will work properly again.  I can't recall experiencing this with PC keyboards, but that's because the damn keyboard interfaces change often enough that I get keyboards every once in a while.  You know, there was the PC, AT, PS/2 and now the USB interface for keyboards.  I don't use my PC keyboards LONG enough for them to wear out!

10427:
Mike Garber wrote:
>>
Does anyone know off-hand of any Astrocade (action) games that actively use the Keypad as part of the controls? Just curious...
>>

There are obviously BASIC languages and machine language monitors that use the keypad, but very few games take advantage of the keypad.  Here are some cartridges that do:

1) Fawn Dungeon - In the instructions the weapon is supposed to be selected from the keypad.  I don't think that this was ever implemented-- at least not in the version that is archived.  "Conan the Barbarian" was supposed to have a similar selection system, but this was never implemented either.

2) Life - Pressing any key on the keypad starts the growth cycle once the "organism" is completely drawn.


3) Music Maker - Selects sound volume and other related music changes.

4) Scribbling - This built-in "game" using the keypad to change the size and color of the brush.  This "game" even has its own overlay.

5) Video Story Book - The keyboard does ALL sorts of stuff in this game.  This cartridge probably uses the keyboard more than any other cartridge other than BASIC.

I mistakenly told Mike that "Coloring Book" uses the keyboard... but I think the menu selections are selected with the Knob.

As can be seen from this limited list there are not any officially released cartridges that use the keypad during gameplay in a fast-type game.  I suppose "Fawn Dungeon" and "Conan" meant to use this function, but they never did.

Did I miss any cartridges that use the keypad?

10429:
A short time ago some people were having trouble with some of the zipped archives on BallyAlley.com because the filenames were too long when unzipped.  Well, I just encountered another problem that can occur because of long filenames.  Since people on this site deal with some of these long filenames because of downloaded Astrocade BASIC programs, I thought that I should mention this here.

I did a backup of my data files to an external hard drive and I noticed that there was a difference in the number of files on the backup and the original.  They should, of course, match EXACTLY.  I narrowed the problem down to my Astrocade directory and then finally to some files with extremely long filenames.  According to the Microsoft website, a file that has a path and filename longer than 255 characters can sometimes have misreported filesize and number of files in a directory.  Strangely, even though there were 27 files, Windows XP was reporting that only 9 files existed.  I shorted the path names and then everything was fine.  I'm not sure if this affects other operating systems such as Vista, Windows 7, the Mac OS or *NIX.

This is a pretty weird error and I was a little worried when I first encountered it.  Keep this in mind when dealing with files from BallyAlley or any TOSEC files (as long filenames are typical across the board with this naming convention).

I would think that would be workable, honestly, even with a somewhat poor
condition keypad. Perhaps if you could implement a pause function any time a
key on the keypad is pressed and then the user can confirm the selection of
the correct keypad entry by pressing fire on the controller to return to the
action.

For instance, let's say I want to quaff a potion when a creature is
approaching. I'd try to press the correct key on the keypad, let's say it's
"5". If I hit "5", the game is paused, I see "5" or "Potion" on the screen,
and then I press the fire button to resume because that's what I want and
continue the game in real-time. Let's say instead of "5" I hit "8". I see
that when the game is paused that brought up my inventory, which I didn't
want. I'd then hit "5" to choose the correct option, see "5" or "Potion" on
the screen and then press the fire button to confirm. That would eliminate
both mis-hits and double hits.

Another option of course is to map those keyboard functions as a backup to
the second controller. In that case the player would need either a
reasonable keypad or a working second controller. I think that scenario
would have to apply to the vast majority of active Astrocade users.

If I hit "5", the game is paused, I see "5" or "Potion" on the screen, and then I press the fire button to resume because that's what I want and continue the game in real-time. Let's say instead of "5" I hit "8". I see that when the game is paused that brought up my inventory, which I didn't want. I'd then hit "5" to choose the correct option, see "5" or "Potion" on the screen and then press the fire button to confirm. That would eliminate both mis-hits and double hits.


Another option of course is to map those keyboard functions as a backup to the second controller. In that case the player would need either a reasonable keypad or a working second controller. I think that scenario would have to apply to the vast majority of active Astrocade users.

This posting DOES relate to the Astrocade... but it gets to it in a round-about way, so hang on and read-through...

This week I got a Harmony cartridge for the Atari 2600.  This cart uses an SD card of up to 32GB (!) in size to hold as many games as you want.  Currently mine is holding most of the TOSEC collection and about eighty of the freely available homebrew games (that's about 2,500 different ROMs... though "only" about 600 of those are actually separate games).  The cartridge cost me $60.  At that price the cartridge is an absolute STEAL.  If I were a programmer for the Atari 2600 then this would be the way that I would create homebrew software.

The Harmony cartridge supports all of the current bankswitching schemes up to 32K of "ROM."  I think that it also adds some RAM.  If you're interested, the Harmony manual is available here:

http://harmony.atariage.com/files/harmony_manual_online.pdf

There is a forum for the Harmony cart, here:

http://www.atariage.com/forums/forum/124-harmony-cartridge/

The Harmony cartridge can be ordered here:

http://harmony.atariage.com/order.html

This Harmony cartridge, which is already about two years old, would open new doors in the homebrew community and would make some incredible games available.  For instance, with Bankswitching on the Astroade, games wouldn't be limited to 8K of ROM.  In the Atari 2600 community there is even a "Melody Circuit" board so that games programmed with the Harmony cartridge can take advantage of its many improvements:

http://atariage.com/store/index.php?l=page_view&p=atariage_melody

Let me get this back to the Bally/Astrocade and ask what is on my mind:

1) How come a device like this doesn't exist for the Bally/Astrocade?  Is it a simple lack of interest or is there more to it than that?

2) Does anyone think anything like this could be created for the Astrocade community?

I'm quite interested to hear what people think of this product and how something similar could work for the Astrocade community.

Adam

I'm quite sure such a device can be created (or adapted) to the Astrocade. The only complications I can foresee are related to power requirements, in case the cartridge is powered by the Astrocade itself, without using an additional power source.

A Brazilian guy used to sell a generic "cartridge emulator", which could be used with any console, requiring only a specific cartridge adapter to be built for any given system (connecting data and address lines to the cartridge connector). In this case, the emulator used its own LCD screen for game selection, and required its own power supply. Here you have the basic description and instructions for making an Atari adapter (both in Portuguese, you can use Google Translator):

http://www.victortrucco.com/EmuladordeCartucho/Oemulador/Oemulador.asp

http://www.victortrucco.com/EmuladordeCartucho/Atari2600/tutorial.asp

Unfortunately, it looks like he sold the intellectual property rights to somebody, so this emulator is no longer available.

There used to be the description of a rom emulator at this page (seems to be down right now):

elm-chan.org/works/erom/report_e.html

It used a PC parallel port and some DOS software to upload contents to a RAM IC, which could then emulated 2764, 27128 and 27256 eproms. I think it could be adapted by a knowledgeable person to be a standalone device, using a microcontroller and some software and documentation that is (or used to be) available at the same website.

Hey Adam-

Glad to see this subject come up again as I have asked about the same thing over
the years.  I've been doing my best to keep up with the group's postings these
past few months but unfortunately I've been out of work since November so my

As far as a device like this not existing for the Bally, yes, I think interest
has a lot to do with it.  Most of the multi-carts and now more the flash carts
seem to be produced by people who gravitate to a certain system, at least in
my opinion.  Unless there is a true market for it (say like the Genesis or NES)
where you are guaranteed to sell them, I think it would have to be a true fan of
the system to develop and produce such a cart.  For example, I have flash carts
for the NES, Atari 5200 and ColecoVision.  Here are the respective sites for the
people that produce them:

RetroZone - http://www.retrousb.com/product_info.php?cPath=24&products_id=34

ATARIMAX - http://www.atarimax.com/5200sd/documentation/index.html
                       
                       
http://www.atarimax.com/colecosd/documentation/index.html

Steve Tucker from Atarimax has made both multi-carts, 128-in-1 on board flash
carts and now his latest carts which use SD based flash memory, which makes
loading games much easier (you just load them on the memory card and insert it
into the cartridge).  Although in Steve's case his business seems primarily
Atari, from what I have read in his sites forums the hardware used in his flash
carts was adaptable to the ColecoVision format. 


The other advantage with his ColecoVision SD based cart is that it also mimics
the latest ColecoVision Mega Cart which supports bank switching and memory
images up to 512k.  So if we could say create an SD based flash cart for the
Bally, we would not only have the advantage of a multi-cart to load multiple ROM
images but could also have the advantage of a bank switched cart for larger and
more complex games on the system.  Programmers would no longer be limited to the
8k of space they have now, and, they would also have a way to distribute their
games digitally without having to go the route of actual cart production. 


It would also make it easier during development I would think as you would
simply load the ROM in development instead of having to burn it to an actual
chip. 


I think with the Bally our best bet to have something like this produced
would be with someone like Ken Lill or Mike White, or anyone else with both and
the technical knowledge about the system as well as the interest in it.  A few
years back I would have thrown 8BitDomain into the mix but unfortunately he is
no longer in business.


I think an SD based flash cart as well as some type bank switched cart for
expanded games could definitely be developed for the system, provided someone
has the desire to actually produce them for this system.  I'd even be willing to
work on financing such projects for the system if ayone out there wants to take
a serious crack at it. 


I personally love seeing the old systems pushed beyond their original limits and
would really like to see what the Bally can do "without limits".

-Michael

10464:
The biggest problem with doing a "bank switching" cart for the Bally is the lack
of needed address lines in the cartridge slot. There ate only A0 to A12. to get
to 64 K you will need to have address to the lines A13 - A15. They areonly
addressable through the 50 pin slot in the back, or by elaborate switching
within the cart. I'm not saying it can't be done, but the end product cost may
be prohibitive.
Ken

10469:
Ken Lill wrote:
>>
The biggest problem with doing a "bank switching" cart for the Bally is the lack of needed address lines in the cartridge slot.
>>

On the
Astrocade this idea may be a little confusing because the Astrocade CAN
address more ROM/RAM than is available in the cartridge slot (as Ken is referring to by the additional address lines), but to
address that additional ROM/RAM space would require the device to be
inserted into the expansion port on the back of the unit.  While a two-part system would be pretty neat and would allow up to 56K to be addressed WITHOUT any bankswitching at all, such a system would be expensive and a bit confusing for some users.  To keep things simple for the user, a bankswitched cartridge would work best.

Presented here is the general idea behind bankswitching.  We're looking at it from a software perspective.  I'm not sure how bankswitching is actually done at the hardware level.

First off, Bankswitching doesn't allow the system to "see" more ROM at a time.  Bankswitching allows the programmer access to more ROM, but the system "sees" the maximum amount of ROM at a time.  In this case, the Astrocade would still only be able to see 8K of ROM from $2000 - $3FFF.  However, with bankswitching, this a ROM larger than 8K could be broken up into small units.  So, a contiguous amount of 8K would be available, but parts of that ROM could be switched in and out at the programmers desire.  Let's say that a 64K ROM was used in an Astrocade cartridge.  The 64K could be broken down into 4K pieces and mapped to the Astrocade like this:

$2000 - $2FFF - 4K always available, and always the same ROM "seen" by the Astrocade
$3000 - $3FFF - 4K Bankswitched ROM.  This area of ROM could be switched out with
                other 4K chunks of the ROM available on the 64K chip.

In this example, the first 4K of the Astrocade cart would be a main program and the other fifteen banks would be switched out at any time by circuitry on the cartridge itself.  These other fifteen banks could be additional program subroutines, program data (graphics), or anything that the programer desires.

A bankswitched cart could be setup in any manner.  The Harmony cartridge for the Atari 2600 console supports nineteen bankswitching techniques by various companies (and can be programmed to support others).

On the Astrocade a bankswitching cart doesn't have to be setup as I described above.  It really is up to the programmer and the person who makes the cartridge.  Let's say Michael Garber makes a new game that he feels would work best with a 6K bank of ROM from $2000-$37FF.  Now, he will have 29 banks of 2K to switch out within that 2K of ROM space from $3800-$3FFF.

There really is no perfect bankswitching technique.  It depends on the programmer and the program being written.

Does this make sense?

>>
I'm not saying it can't be done, but the end product cost may be prohibitive.
>>

New hardware would HAVE to be used in order to keep the costs down.  The Harmony cartridge for the Atari 2600 cost me $60.  Other SD devices for other consoles can cost as much as $150.  An SD cartridge is a cartridge for a USER, not a collector.  A collector will always want the original cartridges, while a user just wants to play the games or use the software and isn't interested in the way that the software is loaded into the host machine... just as long as it works, is easy to use and isn't too expensive.

The biggest problem with doing a "bank switching" cart for the Bally is the lack
of needed address lines in the cartridge slot. There ate only A0 to A12. to get
to 64 K you will need to have address to the lines A13 - A15. They areonly
addressable through the 50 pin slot in the back, or by elaborate switching
within the cart. I'm not saying it can't be done, but the end product cost may
be prohibitive.

You are correct; there are a few simple direct commands to type in order to get the program to load.  In order to load a game from "tape" (in this case, from a WAV file on a PC), type in:

:INPUT

When the program is finished loading (it takes about twenty seconds), type:

RUN

Let's see here, if you don't have an overlay, then that would be:

+,=,2,C [Translation - :, WORDS-KEY, INPUT, GO]

That will load the tape program.  Then type:

Down-Arrow, C [Translation - RUN, GO]

Obviously, the overlay will make this MUCH, MUCH easier.  As you suggested, the overlays ARE available online, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/keypad_overlays/keypad_overlays.html

If you print this overlay from within a browser, then the size will probably be totally wrong (usually it will take up a whole sheet of paper).  That's obviously NOT what you want at all.  The easiest way for a Windows user to print this overlay at actual size is to save the 300-DPI version to your hard drive.  Then, open it with Microsoft Paint and print it (ideally) to a color printer.  I just tried this, to make sure it works properly and it does.  The overlay printout and the actual overlay are EXACTLY the same size.

>>
I've also thought about recording some of the games and posting on YouTube - I have an Eye TV which worked really well to grab the games.

You also have to hit the blue shift to get a colon, so:

That will load the tape program.  Then type:



=,Down-Arrow, C [Translation - WORDS-SHIFT, RUN, GO]

You can also do it all in one go with :INPUT ;RUN

.,+,=,2,0,3,=,Down-Arrow, C

Some of the BASIC programs will require additional keypad input to play, but many just use the controllers.

It is difficult to compare a potential 128K bankswitched Astrocade cartridge to an Atari 8-bit or C64.  For one thing, both of those systems also had limitations with the cartridge memory area just like the Astrocade.  The limitation was either 8K or 16K, I can't recall (I THINK it was 16K).  For this reason, any cartridges that were larger than this size were bankswitched.  The largest bankswitched cartridge that I'm aware of "back in the day" were 512K carts released in the early nineties for the C64 game system in England.  Both of these systems had MANY bankswitched techniques, which would make creating a new backward compatible Flash cart for either of these systems difficult.  Yet Steve already made a flash cart for the Atari 8-Bit that supports just about ANYTHING that you throw at it... including support for floppy disks running from cartridge!

Remember that 128K Astrocade cartridge would NOT be contiguous memory.  There is not suddenly 128K of ROM sitting out there for the Astrocade to use.  Also, there would be no additional RAM.  You'd still be stuck with the 4K of screen RAM.  With that said, I STILL agree with Lance: "128K would be Gold!"

I remembered that there actually are TWO bankswitching techniques for the "Bally."  Sort of.  These techniques are really for the UV-1, so these would have been supported through the expansion bus.  There was an expansion for 256K of screen RAM.  This was 16 banks of 16K that could be quickly switched for fast animation (pretty neat idea!).  Also, I'm pretty sure that the UV-1 could support up to two 256K EPROM "RAM" drives... but I looked at BallyAlley.com and I can't find support for this (can anyone find it?).  Neither of these methods needs to be supported (not that they COULD be supported via the cart port).  I'm just putting this forward since some bankswitching techniques actually DID exist.  For that matter, the UV-1 could run CP/M.  I don't think I'll be hollering for CP/M support anytime soon.

I have been trying to collect "Interface Age" magazine recently (since PDFs aren't available anywhere, I want to try to scan in some of the issues, notably from 1976-1981).  Last week, along with one issue of "Interface Age" I received several magazines from the 1980's.  A couple of them are "Ahoy!," a magazine for Commodore Computers that was published from 1984-1989.  There is an article in the August 1985 issue called (get this!) "Sputter Pop Hiss Chop Flap Crash Slurp Mash" by Orson Scott Card.  Many of you are probably familiar with this author not from computers but from his science fiction books (most notably the Ender series).  Card also wrote for the classic computer magazines too (maybe he STILL writes about computers... I don't know).  I've seen Card's work in Compute! as well.

What struck me about this article is how it begins:

"There were a couple of guys in Orem, Utah, who used to sing along with the 'Crazy Climber' game.  Not humming, SINGING, in full operatic voices.  It attracted a lot of attention, but the truth is that they were merely doing out loud what we all secretly do in our minds.  The music get to you."

At first I found it amusing that Card knows about "Crazy Climber" at all.  I sometimes get this idea that famous people live in an entirely different universe, but then I read a little tid-bit like this and I realize just how similar the lives are that each of us leads.

10498:
Hi Guys,

Michael Di Salvo over at AtariAge contacted me about the possibility of a bank switched homebrew PCB for making larger Astrocade games.

I've read the discussions so far and taken a look at the Astrocade schematics and executive disassembly.

From what I've seen it should be possible to make a flash programmable homebrew PCB with 128K ROM using a reasonable number of parts.

I haven't laid out a schematic yet, but I believe it should be possible make a PCB that has 32 4K banks and one fixed 4K bank, which would work similarly to 'mega-cart' bank switching on the Colecovision.

I haven't even written any software for the Astrocade, so I'll leave the question open to more experienced people, is 128K enough and is a 4K/4K system workable?

The board I'm thinking of would be organized in z80 memory as:

2000-2FFF (Fixed 4K Region, never changes)
3000-3FFF (Banked 4K Region, can be any of the 32 4K banks)

Bank switching would be done by touching an address at the top of the fixed region, 2FE0..2FFF, with the low 5 bits being latched at the end of the Z80 /RD cycle.

Using smaller banks would require more parts.  I believe a 4K/4K system will fit completely in a GAL22V10 and also accommodate inputs for a second PCB connection so the device can be flash programmed using a Maxflash USB programmer.

If the design only ended up requiring the parts I'm imagining here, a production run of quality assembled boards would probably be in the $12/ea range for a run of 250 pcs.

I'd be happy to lay out a board and give it a try, but I don't actually have a working Astrocade.  If someone has one to loan/sell and is willing to cover the costs of a set of prototype PCBs, I can probably have a set of prototypes ready people in the group to test within a month or two.

Someone would also need to write a z80 program to test the bank switching, which should be extremely simple if you already have code  libraries for displaying data on the screen, etc.

Going to be busy most of the weekend but looking forward to hearing your thoughts.

Steve
